Similarly, in the Synopsis of Dorotheus we read that Aristobulus was made bishop of Britain; and in a fragment published under the name of Heleca, bishop of Saragossa, we find this: "Among the Britons the memory of many martyrs is celebrated, especially of St. Aristobulus, one of the seventy-two disciples, who was also called Zebedee (the father of James and of John the martyr, and of Mary Salome), who went to Rome with Peter. From there, having left his household behind and been sent into England as bishop, he died a martyr in the second year of the most savage emperor Nero." So it reads on page 108 of the Saragossa edition. But the words I have enclosed in parentheses should be corrected to read: "the father of James and John, the husband of Mary Salome." For on the following page, Concordia, the wife of the apostle Peter, is reported to have been the daughter of Aristobulus and Salome. "St. Peter," says the author, "is held in honor in Spain, and his wife Concordia suffered at Rome under Nero, not long before he himself suffered. She was, as M. Maximus teaches in his commentaries on the epistle of St. Peter, the daughter of Aristobulus, or Zebedee, and of Salome; she was also the mother-in-law of Andrew, who married the other sister of Concordia, and of James and John. Now Aristobulus, surnamed Zebedee, was the brother of Barnabas, the apostle of the Lord." So says that author; and the Greeks agree with him concerning Peter's marrying the daughter of Aristobulus, the brother of the apostle Barnabas, both in Metaphrastes, in his commentary on Peter and Paul, and in the Menaia, at the 29th day of June.

At the end of the second epistle to Timothy, the apostle mentions Pudens, Linus, and Claudia together.

Pseudo-Clement intimates that Linus, the first bishop of the Roman Church, ordained by Paul, was the son of Claudia.

But the Liber Pontificalis asserts that the father of Linus was a certain Herculanus.
